immediate_actions: Reset the KRBTGT account password TWICE with a minimum 10-hour gap between resets — this invalidates all forged Golden Tickets domain-wide: Set-ADAccountPassword -Identity krbtgt -Reset -NewPassword (ConvertTo-SecureString -AsPlainText 'Pass1!' -Force) — repeat with a different password after 10 hours

Audit EID 4769 for RC4 encryption (0x17) with anomalous ticket options (0x40810000) or lifetimes exceeding 10 hours: wevtutil qe Security "/q:*[EventData[Data[@Name='TicketEncryptionType']='0x17']]" /f:text /c:200
Enable Kerberos service ticket audit immediately: auditpol /set /subcategory:"Kerberos Service Ticket Operations" /success:enable /failure:enable
Identify all systems where forged tickets may have been used by cross-referencing EID 4624/4648 logon events from the compromise window against non-DC source IPs
short_term_actions: Deploy Microsoft Defender for Identity (MDI) or equivalent to detect anomalous Kerberos ticket requests in real time
Enforce AES-only Kerberos encryption for all privileged accounts: Set-ADUser -Identity <user> -KerberosEncryptionType AES128,AES256
Audit all privileged group memberships for unauthorized changes since the earliest known compromise timestamp
Rotate ALL service account and admin account passwords — treat the entire domain credential store as compromised
prevention: Restrict access to Domain Controllers to Tier 0 accounts only via a tiered administration model (Tier 0/1/2)
Rotate the KRBTGT password every 180 days as standard operating procedure
Enable Protected Users security group for all privileged accounts to disable RC4 downgrade attacks
Deploy Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs) for all Tier 0 administrative tasks
accounts_at_risk: All domain accounts — KRBTGT compromise allows impersonation of any user in the domain

immediate_actions: Reset the computer account password for each affected host to invalidate Silver Tickets forged with the machine account hash: Reset-ComputerMachinePassword (run on affected host, or use: Set-ADComputer -Identity <host> -KerberosEncryptionType AES128,AES256)
Reset passwords for all service accounts targeted by Silver Tickets — check service names (CIFS, HTTP, RPCSS, LDAP, HOST) in EID 4769 ServiceName field

Audit EID 4769 events WITHOUT a preceding EID 4768 from the same user within 20 minutes — this TGT-bypass pattern is the primary Silver Ticket indicator: wevtutil qe Security "/q:*[EventData[Data[@Name='ServiceName']!='krbtgt']]" /f:text | findstr /i 0x17
Enable Kerberos logging: auditpol /set /subcategory:"Kerberos Authentication Service" /success:enable /failure:enable
short_term_actions: Enable AES-only encryption for all service accounts and computer accounts to eliminate RC4 as a Silver Ticket vector
Deploy Microsoft Defender for Identity to detect forged service ticket attacks via Kerberos behavioral analytics
Audit all SPNs to identify which services were targeted: Get-ADComputer -Filter * -Properties ServicePrincipalName | Where {$_.ServicePrincipalName}
Review all access logs for targeted services during the incident window for signs of unauthorized data access or lateral movement
prevention: Add all service accounts to the Protected Users security group — disables RC4 and enforces AES
Rotate all computer account passwords and service account passwords every 90 days
Segment services so a Silver Ticket for one service cannot pivot to other high-value services
Configure Kerberos Armoring (FAST) via Group Policy to protect ticket exchange
accounts_at_risk: Service accounts and computer accounts for targeted services (CIFS, HTTP, LDAP, RPCSS, HOST)

immediate_actions: Identify all SPN-bearing accounts immediately: Get-ADUser -Filter {ServicePrincipalName -ne '$null'} -Properties ServicePrincipalName,PasswordLastSet | Select Name,SamAccountName,PasswordLastSet,ServicePrincipalName | Export-Csv spn_accounts.csv
Rotate passwords for ALL SPN-bearing accounts immediately — assume all RC4 hashes have been captured and are being cracked offline

Detect Kerberoasting activity via EID 4769 with RC4 (0x17) and unusual volume: Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security';Id=4769} | Where {$_.Message -like '*0x17*'} | Group {$_.Properties[2].Value} | Sort Count -Descending | Select -First 20
Enable Kerberos service ticket audit: auditpol /set /subcategory:"Kerberos Service Ticket Operations" /success:enable /failure:enable
short_term_actions: Enforce AES-256 encryption for all service accounts: Set-ADUser -Identity <svc_acct> -KerberosEncryptionType AES128,AES256 — removes RC4 as a crackable hash type
Enforce minimum 25-character randomly-generated passwords for all service accounts
Migrate service accounts to Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA) — auto-rotating 240-character passwords make Kerberoasting computationally infeasible
Deploy a honeypot SPN account with alerting on any TGS request against it
prevention: Use Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA) for all services — gMSA passwords rotate automatically every 30 days
Audit SPN registrations quarterly — any user-attached SPN is a Kerberoasting target
Create a standing SIEM detection: EID 4769 with encryption type 0x17 from a non-service-account source, volume >10 per minute
accounts_at_risk: All Active Directory user accounts with registered Service Principal Names (SPNs)

immediate_actions: Identify all accounts with pre-authentication disabled: Get-ADUser -Filter {DoesNotRequirePreAuth -eq $True} -Properties DoesNotRequirePreAuth | Select Name,SamAccountName,DistinguishedName
Re-enable Kerberos pre-authentication for all identified accounts: Set-ADUser -Identity <user> -KerberosPreAuthRequired $True
Rotate passwords for all accounts that had pre-authentication disabled — their AS-REP hashes have been captured
Search for GetNPUsers, Rubeus asreproast, or bulk EID 4768 requests with RC4 pre-auth type as Kerberoasting tool indicators
short_term_actions: Audit all accounts with UF_DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH flag quarterly — this flag should never be set on standard accounts
Set minimum 20+ character passwords for any account that legitimately requires pre-auth disabled
Enable EID 4768 audit: auditpol /set /subcategory:"Kerberos Authentication Service" /failure:enable
prevention: Never disable Kerberos pre-authentication unless operationally required — document and review all exceptions quarterly
Create a SIEM alert for account modification (EID 4738) that disables pre-authentication: flag UserParameters changes setting UF_DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH
accounts_at_risk: All Active Directory accounts with Kerberos pre-authentication disabled (DoesNotRequirePreAuth = True)

immediate_actions: Add all privileged accounts to the Protected Users security group to disable NTLM: Add-ADGroupMember -Identity 'Protected Users' -Members <admin_account>

Restrict outgoing NTLM via GPO immediately: Computer Config > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > 'Network security: Restrict NTLM: Outgoing NTLM traffic to remote servers' = Deny All
Set NTLM compatibility to NTLMv2 only: reg add HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa /v LmCompatibilityLevel /t REG_DWORD /d 5 /f
Rotate NTLM credentials (passwords) for ALL accounts in the lateral movement chain — the NTLM hash is the credential
short_term_actions: Enable Credential Guard via Group Policy: Computer Config > Admin Templates > System > Device Guard > Turn On Virtualization Based Security > enable with Secure Boot and DMA protection
Enable LAPS on all workstations to randomize local admin passwords per machine, eliminating shared local credential lateral movement
Audit NTLM usage across the environment to find remaining NTLM dependencies before enforcing full restriction
Review EID 4624 Logon Type 3 and EID 4648 (Explicit Credential Use) for anomalous lateral movement from the incident window
prevention: Deploy Windows Defender Credential Guard on all supported systems (Windows 10/Server 2016+)
Enforce Kerberos-only authentication for all internal services — disable NTLM on Domain Controllers via GPO
Implement network microsegmentation to limit the blast radius of credential theft
Use tiered administration model so PTH in one tier cannot compromise another
accounts_at_risk: All accounts whose NTLM hashes were cached on compromised systems (local accounts, domain accounts with interactive logon history)

immediate_actions: Purge all Kerberos tickets on every affected host: klist purge — must be run on each compromised system to invalidate in-memory tickets
If a Golden Ticket is the ticket source, reset KRBTGT password TWICE with a 10-hour gap
If Silver Tickets are suspected, reset the service account passwords and computer account passwords for targeted services
Search for Rubeus, mimikatz kerberos::ptt, .kirbi, and .ccache files: Get-ChildItem -Recurse -Include *.kirbi,*.ccache C:\ 2>$null | Select FullName,LastWriteTime
short_term_actions: Enable Kerberos ticket monitoring: audit EID 4768 (TGT) and EID 4769 (TGS) — tickets used without a prior TGT request indicate Pass-the-Ticket
Deploy Microsoft Defender for Identity — Pass-the-Ticket detection is built-in via Kerberos anomaly analysis
Restrict Kerberos ticket lifetime to 8 hours maximum in Default Domain Policy
prevention: Enable Protected Users security group for all privileged accounts (enforces AES-only, 4-hour ticket lifetime)
Deploy PAM with just-in-time privilege so privileged Kerberos tickets are never left persisted in memory
Segment the network so stolen tickets cannot reach high-value services from attacker-controlled hosts
accounts_at_risk: Accounts whose Kerberos tickets were stolen from memory on compromised systems — typically privileged accounts

immediate_actions: Enable LSASS Protected Process Light (PPL) immediately: reg add HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa /v RunAsPPL /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f — requires reboot; blocks most LSASS dump tools

Rotate ALL domain credentials — treat every password cached in LSASS on affected systems as compromised: service accounts, domain admin accounts, and any user with an interactive logon in the past 90 days
Search for LSASS dump files: Get-ChildItem -Path C:\ -Recurse -Include lsass*.dmp,lsass.exe.* -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue — quarantine any found

Review Sysmon EID 10 (process access on lsass.exe) from the incident window to identify all dump tool processes: Get-WinEvent -Path *.evtx | Where {$_.Id -eq 10 -and $_.Properties[4].Value -like '*lsass*'}
short_term_actions: Enable Windows Defender Credential Guard on all systems (requires UEFI Secure Boot + VBS)
Enable ASR rule to block credential stealing from LSASS: Set-MpPreference -AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Ids 9e6c4e1f-7d60-472f-ba1a-a39ef669e4b0 -AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Actions Enabled
Disable WDigest to prevent plaintext credential caching: reg add HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\WDigest /v UseLogonCredential /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
Deploy LAPS for all workstations — prevents lateral movement via shared local admin credentials
prevention: Enable Credential Guard and PPL as a baseline configuration for all Windows endpoints via Group Policy
Restrict local administrator rights — only accounts that operationally require them should have them
Create Sysmon alerting rule for EID 10 (process access) targeting lsass.exe from non-system processes
accounts_at_risk: All accounts with active sessions or cached credentials on the compromised host at the time of the dump

immediate_actions: Audit who holds DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All rights immediately: (Get-Acl 'AD:\DC=yourdomain,DC=com').Access | Where {$_.ObjectType -eq '1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2'} | Select IdentityReference,AccessControlType
Remove unauthorized replication rights via ADSI Edit: navigate to domain root object > Properties > Security > Advanced > remove DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All from any non-DC account
Reset the KRBTGT password TWICE with a 10-hour gap — DCSync recovers the krbtgt hash enabling Golden Ticket attacks
Rotate ALL privileged account passwords in Tier 0 (Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, Schema Admins) immediately — treat full domain credential store as compromised
short_term_actions: Enable Directory Service Access auditing: auditpol /set /subcategory:"Directory Service Access" /success:enable — generates EID 4662 for replication right use
Create a SIEM rule: EID 4662 with ObjectType 1131f6ad (Replicating Directory Changes All) from any non-Domain-Controller IP is a DCSync alert
Deploy Microsoft Defender for Identity — DCSync detection is a built-in alert (fires on EID 4662 from non-DC)
Review all accounts granted replication rights in the past 90 days via EID 4728/4756
prevention: Limit DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All rights to Domain Controller computer accounts only — never user accounts
Deploy tiered admin model ensuring no account used interactively on workstations holds DC replication rights
Standing SIEM alert: EID 4662 with ObjectType 1131f6ad from a non-DC source IP
accounts_at_risk: Entire Active Directory — DCSync recovers all password hashes in the domain including the KRBTGT hash

immediate_actions: Reboot all Domain Controllers IMMEDIATELY — the Skeleton Key patch is in-memory only and does not survive a reboot: this is the fastest remediation for the active backdoor
After reboot, reset KRBTGT password TWICE (10-hour gap) and rotate ALL privileged account passwords — attacker likely captured hashes before deploying the skeleton key
Search for misc::skeleton execution artifacts in EDR/Sysmon telemetry from the incident window: look for lsass.exe memory write operations from unexpected processes
Audit all Domain Controller logon events since the earliest compromise timestamp for logins using unusual credentials (skeleton key default password is 'mimikatz')
short_term_actions: Enable LSASS PPL on all Domain Controllers: reg add HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa /v RunAsPPL /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
Enable Credential Guard on all Domain Controllers (Server 2016+)
Deploy integrity monitoring on the LSASS module list to detect future in-memory patching attempts
Review all domain authentications since the compromise window — any successful auth with invalid credentials indicates active skeleton key use
prevention: Deploy Microsoft Defender for Identity — Skeleton Key detection monitors for LSASS patching patterns
Enable Secure Boot and TPM on all Domain Controllers to ensure boot chain integrity
Restrict physical and hypervisor-level access to Domain Controllers to Tier 0 administrators only
accounts_at_risk: All domain accounts — Skeleton Key allows authentication as any user with a master backdoor password while leaving normal passwords functional

immediate_actions: Block direct inbound RDP at the perimeter firewall — all RDP must route through a jump server or RD Gateway: New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName 'Block Direct RDP' -Direction Inbound -Protocol TCP -LocalPort 3389 -Action Block
Enable Network Level Authentication (NLA): Set-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server\WinStations\RDP-Tcp' -Name SecurityLayer -Value 2 -Type DWord

Audit all RDP sessions in the incident window (Logon Type 10): Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security';Id=4624} | Where {$_.Properties[8].Value -eq 10} | Select TimeCreated,@{N='User';E={$_.Properties[5].Value}},@{N='SourceIP';E={$_.Properties[18].Value}}
Disable RDP on all hosts where it is not operationally required: Set-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server' -Name fDenyTSConnections -Value 1
short_term_actions: Deploy Microsoft Remote Desktop Gateway (RD Gateway) as the sole RDP entry point — enforces MFA and provides centralized audit logging
Restrict RDP by source IP at Windows Firewall: New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName 'RDP Jump Server Only' -Direction Inbound -Protocol TCP -LocalPort 3389 -RemoteAddress <jumpserver_ip> -Action Allow
Enable EID 4778 (session reconnect) and EID 4779 (session disconnect) forwarding to SIEM
prevention: Enforce MFA for all RDP sessions via RD Gateway or Conditional Access
Implement JIT (Just-In-Time) access for RDP via Microsoft Defender for Cloud or a PAM solution
Use Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs) for all RDP-based administration
accounts_at_risk: All accounts with Remote Desktop Users group membership on affected hosts: Get-LocalGroupMember -Group 'Remote Desktop Users'

immediate_actions: Enable SMB signing on all systems to prevent relay attacks: Set-SmbServerConfiguration -RequireSecuritySignature $True -Force && Set-SmbClientConfiguration -RequireSecuritySignature $True -Force

Audit admin share connections from the incident window: Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security';Id=5140} | Where {$_.Properties[6].Value -match 'ADMIN\$|C\$|IPC\$|D\$'} | Select TimeCreated,@{N='User';E={$_.Properties[1].Value}},@{N='Share';E={$_.Properties[6].Value}},@{N='SourceIP';E={$_.Properties[8].Value}}
Terminate all active unauthorized admin share sessions: net session \\<attacker_ip> /delete
Block SMB (TCP 445) between workstations at the firewall — workstations should communicate with file servers, not each other
short_term_actions: Disable admin shares on workstations where not required: reg add HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\Parameters /v AutoShareWks /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
Enable SMB file share audit: auditpol /set /subcategory:"File Share" /success:enable /failure:enable — generates EID 5140/5145
Deploy LAPS on all workstations so local admin passwords are unique per machine
prevention: Implement host-based firewall rules blocking lateral SMB (TCP 445/139) between endpoint segments via GPO
Require Kerberos authentication for all SMB connections — disable NTLM fallback for SMB
Audit admin share usage as a standing SIEM detection: EID 5140 with share name matching ADMIN$/C$/D$ from non-standard source IPs
accounts_at_risk: Accounts used to connect to admin shares — typically local administrators or domain admins on affected hosts

immediate_actions: Disable WinRM on all hosts where it is not operationally required: Disable-PSRemoting -Force && Stop-Service winrm -PassThru | Set-Service -StartupType Disabled

Restrict WinRM access to authorized management hosts via firewall: New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName 'WinRM Allow Mgmt Only' -Direction Inbound -Protocol TCP -LocalPort 5985,5986 -RemoteAddress <mgmt_host_ip> -Action Allow

Audit all PowerShell remoting sessions in the incident window: Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational';Id=400,403} | Select TimeCreated,@{N='Details';E={$_.Message.Substring(0,200)}}
Enumerate active WinRM sessions: Get-WSManInstance -ResourceURI shell -Enumerate | Select Owner,ProcessID,ShellRunTime
short_term_actions: Enable WinRM over HTTPS only (port 5986) with certificate authentication — disable HTTP (port 5985): winrm set winrm/config/listener @{Transport='HTTPS';CertificateThumbprint='<thumbprint>'}
Configure WinRM to require Kerberos only: winrm set winrm/config/service/auth @{Kerberos='true';Basic='false';Negotiate='false'}
Enable PowerShell Script Block Logging to capture all WinRM-delivered commands
prevention: Use JEA (Just Enough Administration) endpoints to restrict which cmdlets can run via WinRM
Enforce Constrained Language Mode for non-administrative WinRM sessions
Forward WinRM connection events to SIEM and alert on connections from non-management hosts
accounts_at_risk: Accounts with WinRM access on affected hosts — check via: (Get-PSSessionConfiguration -Name Microsoft.PowerShell).Permission

immediate_actions: Enable WMI Activity logging: auditpol /set /subcategory:"WMI Activity" /success:enable — generates events in Microsoft-Windows-WMI-Activity/Operational

Enumerate all WMI subscriptions for persistence (common technique): Get-WMIObject -Namespace root\subscription -Class __EventFilter | Select Name,Query; Get-WMIObject -Namespace root\subscription -Class __EventConsumer | Select Name; Get-WMIObject -Namespace root\subscription -Class __FilterToConsumerBinding
Remove any unauthorized WMI subscriptions: Get-WMIObject -Namespace root\subscription -Class __FilterToConsumerBinding | Remove-WmiObject
Block remote WMI access at the firewall between workstations: block TCP 135 (RPC Endpoint Mapper) and DCOM dynamic ports (49152-65535)
short_term_actions: Deploy Sysmon with WMI event subscription monitoring (Sysmon EID 19, 20, 21) to detect persistent WMI consumers
Restrict WMI namespace permissions to administrators only: use wmimgmt.msc to audit and restrict namespace security
Review Microsoft-Windows-WMI-Activity/Operational log for lateral WMI execution entries from the incident window
prevention: Apply WDAC policies to block unauthorized WMI consumers
Segment the network so workstations cannot initiate WMI connections to other workstations
Create SIEM detections for WMI subscription creation (Sysmon EID 19/20/21) from non-admin accounts
accounts_at_risk: Accounts with WMI remote access rights — restrict via DCOM security settings in Component Services (dcomcnfg)

immediate_actions: Enable PowerShell Script Block Logging: reg add HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ScriptBlockLogging /v EnableScriptBlockLogging /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f

Enable PowerShell Module Logging: reg add HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ModuleLogging /v EnableModuleLogging /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f && reg add HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ModuleLogging\ModuleNames /v * /t REG_SZ /d * /f
Disable PowerShell v2 to prevent AMSI and logging bypass: Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName MicrosoftWindowsPowerShellV2Root -NoRestart

Review all EID 4104 (Script Block logged) events from the incident window for encoded commands and malicious payloads: Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational';Id=4104} | Where {$_.Message -like '*encodedcommand*' -or $_.Message -like '*frombase64*'}
short_term_actions: Enforce AllSigned or RemoteSigned execution policy: Set-ExecutionPolicy AllSigned -Scope LocalMachine -Force
Enable PowerShell Constrained Language Mode for non-administrative accounts via AppLocker or WDAC
Enable PowerShell Transcription: reg add HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\Transcription /v EnableTranscripting /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
prevention: Deploy AppLocker or WDAC policies restricting which accounts can run PowerShell.exe and PowerShell_ISE.exe
Route all administrative PowerShell to JEA endpoints to limit available cmdlets per role
Forward all EID 4103/4104 Script Block events to SIEM with high-entropy string detection rules
accounts_at_risk: Accounts that executed malicious PowerShell during the incident — verify via EID 4103/4104 SubjectUserName field

immediate_actions: Enable process creation audit with command line logging: auditpol /set /subcategory:"Process Creation" /success:enable && reg add HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\Audit /v ProcessCreationIncludeCmdLine_Enabled /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f

Review all cmd.exe executions from the incident window for malicious command sequences: Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security';Id=4688} | Where {$_.Properties[5].Value -like '*cmd.exe*'} | Select TimeCreated,@{N='CmdLine';E={$_.Properties[8].Value}},@{N='User';E={$_.Properties[1].Value}}
Search for cmd.exe /c commands spawned from unusual parent processes (Office, browsers, web servers) via Sysmon EID 1

Identify and quarantine any scripts or batch files dropped during the incident: Get-ChildItem -Recurse -Include *.bat,*.cmd C:\Windows\Temp,C:\Users -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Where {$_.LastWriteTime -gt (Get-Date).AddDays(-14)}
short_term_actions: Deploy Sysmon with parent-child process relationship logging to detect cmd.exe spawned from abnormal parents
Implement AppLocker rules restricting cmd.exe execution for end users
Alert on cmd.exe /c invocations containing download indicators: certutil, bitsadmin, curl, wget, powershell -enc
prevention: Block cmd.exe for standard users via AppLocker Publisher or Path rules
Use WDAC to enforce script execution restrictions
Deploy EDR with behavioral detection for command-shell abuse (living-off-the-land patterns)
accounts_at_risk: Accounts that executed malicious commands — check EID 4688 SubjectUserName from the incident window

immediate_actions: Verify AMSI is operational on all affected hosts — check AMSI provider registration: Get-MpThreatDetection | Select AMSIProtectionTriggered, ThreatName | Where {$_.AMSIProtectionTriggered}

Enable Deep Script Block Logging to capture obfuscated payload content at execution time: reg add HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ScriptBlockLogging /v EnableScriptBlockInvocationLogging /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
Extract and analyze all EID 4104 Script Block events from the incident window — look for: fromBase64String, -join [char], AmsiUtils, amsiinitfailed, [System.Reflection.Assembly]::Load
Scan affected systems for encoded payloads: Get-ChildItem -Recurse C:\Windows\Temp,C:\Users -Include *.ps1,*.vbs,*.js | Where {$_.Length -gt 5000} | Select FullName,LastWriteTime
short_term_actions: Block PowerShell v2 (bypasses AMSI and ScriptBlock logging entirely): Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName MicrosoftWindowsPowerShellV2Root
Deploy EDR with script content analysis (CrowdStrike, SentinelOne, Defender ATP) to detect obfuscated payload execution in real time
Enable AMSI integration for VBScript and JScript: verify registry: HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\AMSI\Providers
prevention: Enforce Constrained Language Mode via AppLocker to block reflection-based AMSI bypasses
Create a SIEM detection rule: EID 4104 events containing strings 'AmsiUtils', 'amsiinitfailed', 'amsiscanbuffer', or base64 blobs >50 characters
Deploy WDAC to block unsigned or untrusted script execution
accounts_at_risk: Accounts that executed obfuscated scripts — verify via EID 4104 SubjectUserName field from the incident window

immediate_actions: Disable all accounts involved in unauthorized access: Disable-ADAccount -Identity <username> — do not delete; preserve for forensic review
Invalidate all active Kerberos tickets and sessions for involved accounts: klist purge (on affected hosts); revoke all OAuth tokens if cloud-connected

Force password reset for all involved accounts: Set-ADAccountPassword -Identity <user> -Reset -NewPassword (ConvertTo-SecureString -AsPlainText 'NewPass!' -Force) && Set-ADUser -Identity <user> -ChangePasswordAtLogon $True
Audit all logon events (EID 4624) for affected accounts in the 30 days prior to detection — establish the true compromise start time, not just detection time
short_term_actions: Enforce MFA for all accounts via Conditional Access or on-premises MFA proxy — especially privileged accounts
Review and disable stale accounts: Search-ADAccount -AccountInactive -TimeSpan 90.00:00:00 | Select Name,LastLogonDate — disable all accounts inactive for 90+ days
Enable account lockout policy: 5 failed attempts, 15-minute lockout, 30-minute observation window
Deploy risky sign-in detection via Azure AD Identity Protection or equivalent on-premises tool
prevention: Implement privileged account lifecycle process: review quarterly, disable when no longer needed
Require hardware MFA tokens (FIDO2) for all privileged domain accounts
Deploy a SIEM alert on logon from new geolocation, outside business hours, or via anonymizing proxies
accounts_at_risk: All accounts that authenticated during the incident window — review EID 4624/4648 for the complete list

immediate_actions: Enumerate all tasks created or modified during the incident window: Get-ScheduledTask | Where {$_.Date -gt (Get-Date).AddDays(-30)} | Select TaskName,TaskPath,Date,@{N='RunAs';E={$_.Principal.UserId}},@{N='Command';E={($_.Actions | Select -First 1).Execute}} | Sort Date -Descending
Remove all unauthorized tasks immediately: Unregister-ScheduledTask -TaskName '<taskname>' -Confirm:$false

Search for tasks running from suspicious paths: Get-ScheduledTask | Select -ExpandProperty Actions | Where {$_.Execute -like '*AppData*' -or $_.Execute -like '*Temp*' -or $_.Execute -like '*Public*'} | Select Execute,Arguments
Verify EID 4698 (Task Created) and EID 4702 (Task Modified) audit is enabled: auditpol /set /subcategory:"Other Object Access Events" /success:enable
short_term_actions: Forward EID 4698/4702/4699/4700 to SIEM with alerting on task creation outside approved change windows
Restrict scheduled task creation to administrators only via Group Policy: User Rights Assignment > 'Log on as a batch job'
Enable Sysmon to log process creation events where parent is Task Scheduler (svchost.exe -k netsvcs -p -s Schedule)
prevention: Baseline all scheduled tasks per system type and alert on any new task deviating from baseline
Use AppLocker to restrict which executables can be launched by Task Scheduler
Alert on schtasks.exe and at.exe invocations from non-administrative processes via Sysmon
accounts_at_risk: Accounts configured in task RunAs settings — check task Principal.UserId for the execution context of each suspicious task

immediate_actions: Enumerate services created during the incident window: Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='System';Id=7045} | Select TimeCreated,@{N='Service';E={$_.Properties[0].Value}},@{N='Path';E={$_.Properties[1].Value}},@{N='StartType';E={$_.Properties[2].Value}} | Sort TimeCreated -Descending
Stop and remove unauthorized services: sc.exe stop <service_name> && sc.exe delete <service_name>

Audit all service binary paths for services running from user-writable locations: Get-WmiObject Win32_Service | Where {$_.PathName -like '*Temp*' -or $_.PathName -like '*AppData*' -or $_.PathName -like '*Users*'} | Select Name,PathName,StartMode,StartName
Enable Service Control Manager audit if not already active: auditpol /set /subcategory:"Security System Extension" /success:enable — creates EID 4697
short_term_actions: Baseline all services per system type and maintain an allowlist — any new service triggers a SIEM alert
Restrict service creation to SYSTEM and built-in Administrators only via security policy
Review EID 7045 and EID 4697 for the past 30 days to identify all persistence services installed
prevention: Use WDAC to block unsigned service binaries from executing
Restrict sc.exe execution for non-administrative users via AppLocker
Create a SIEM alert on EID 7045 and EID 4697 outside of approved change windows
accounts_at_risk: Accounts that installed malicious services — check EID 4697 SubjectAccountName field for the installer identity

immediate_actions: Audit all Run and RunOnce keys for unauthorized entries: reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run; reg query HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run; reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce; reg query HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce
Remove unauthorized persistence entries: reg delete HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run /v <value_name> /f
Check startup folders for malicious entries: Get-ChildItem 'C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\StartUp'; Get-ChildItem "$env:APPDATA\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup"
Enable registry auditing on Run keys: set a SACL via Regedit > HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run > Permissions > Advanced > Auditing — generates EID 4657
short_term_actions: Deploy Sysmon with registry monitoring rules to alert on modifications to Run/RunOnce keys (Sysmon EID 12, 13, 14)
Baseline all Run key values per system type and forward changes to SIEM
Restrict registry write access to Run keys for non-administrator accounts via Group Policy
prevention: Use AppLocker or SRP to prevent unauthorized executables from launching at startup
Monitor EID 4657 (Registry value modified) for Run key changes via Windows Security audit
Deploy an EDR with registry persistence detection and automated rollback capabilities
accounts_at_risk: Accounts active on the affected system at next boot — persistence executes in the context of the logged-on user or SYSTEM

immediate_actions: Enumerate all accounts created during the incident window: Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security';Id=4720} | Select TimeCreated,@{N='NewAccount';E={$_.Properties[0].Value}},@{N='CreatedBy';E={$_.Properties[4].Value}},@{N='Domain';E={$_.Properties[1].Value}}
Disable and delete all unauthorized accounts immediately: Disable-LocalUser -Name <backdoor_account>; Remove-LocalUser -Name <backdoor_account>

Check if new accounts were added to privileged groups: Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security';Id=4732,4728} | Where {$_.TimeCreated -gt (Get-Date).AddDays(-30)} | Select TimeCreated,Message
Verify no unauthorized accounts exist in local Administrators group on any affected host: Get-LocalGroupMember -Group Administrators
short_term_actions: Enable EID 4720 forwarding to SIEM with alerting on all new account creation, especially outside change windows
Implement a formal account provisioning process requiring documented approval before any account creation
Audit all local administrator group memberships across the environment using LAPS reporting or Entra ID
prevention: Restrict local account creation to domain administrators via User Rights Assignment GPO
Block local account logon on domain-joined systems to enforce domain account usage
Deploy a SIEM alert on EID 4720 at any time — local account creation is rare in managed environments
accounts_at_risk: The newly created backdoor accounts — disable immediately; also investigate the account that created them (EID 4720 SubjectAccountName)

immediate_actions: Audit all group membership changes in the incident window: Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security';Id=4728,4732,4756} | Select TimeCreated,@{N='AddedAccount';E={$_.Properties[0].Value}},@{N='Group';E={$_.Properties[2].Value}},@{N='ChangedBy';E={$_.Properties[4].Value}}
Remove all unauthorized accounts from privileged groups immediately: Remove-ADGroupMember -Identity 'Domain Admins' -Members <backdoor_account> -Confirm:$false
Review all privileged group memberships right now: Get-ADGroupMember -Identity 'Domain Admins' -Recursive | Select Name,SamAccountName,DistinguishedName — compare to approved membership list
Reset credentials for legitimate accounts used to make unauthorized group membership changes
short_term_actions: Enable privileged group change alerting in SIEM: EID 4728 (Domain Admin group change) should trigger immediate paging outside change windows
Deploy Microsoft Defender for Identity alert: 'Account added to sensitive group' (built-in detection)
Implement Privileged Identity Management (PIM) with time-limited, approval-based group membership elevation
prevention: Use PIM/PAM with time-bound group membership so no account has standing Domain Admin rights
Set AdminSDHolder propagation monitoring — privileged group ACLs should not change unexpectedly
Audit privileged group memberships weekly and compare against an approved membership list
accounts_at_risk: All accounts added to privileged groups — these accounts now have elevated rights that must be revoked immediately

immediate_actions: Audit all GPO changes in the incident window: Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security';Id=5136} | Where {$_.Properties[1].Value -like '*GroupPolicyContainer*'} | Select TimeCreated,@{N='Object';E={$_.Properties[8].Value}},@{N='ChangedBy';E={$_.Properties[3].Value}}
Run gpresult /h gpo_report.html on affected systems and compare to a known-good GPO baseline to identify all unauthorized settings
Revert unauthorized GPO changes via Group Policy Management Console — restore from backup if available: Restore-GPO -Name '<GPO Name>' -Path C:\GPOBackup
Audit all accounts with GPO edit/modify permissions: Get-GPPermissions -All -Name <gpo_name> | Where {$_.Permission -in 'GpoEdit','GpoEditDeleteModifySecurity'} | Select Trustee,Permission
short_term_actions: Enable Directory Service Changes audit: auditpol /set /subcategory:"Directory Service Changes" /success:enable — generates EID 5136 on DCs for all AD object changes including GPOs
Backup all current GPO configurations immediately: Backup-Gpo -All -Path C:\GPO_Backup_$(Get-Date -Format yyyyMMdd)
Deploy AGPM (Advanced Group Policy Management) to enforce approval workflow for all GPO modifications
prevention: Delegate GPO editing rights only to specific named administrators — never to generic groups or all Domain Admins
Enable SIEM alert: EID 5136 with objectClass=groupPolicyContainer outside change windows
Test GPO changes in a staging OU before applying to production via AGPM
accounts_at_risk: All domain systems affected by the modified GPOs — scope determined by GPO link structure; run gpresult to assess blast radius

immediate_actions: Take the exploited application OFFLINE or apply emergency WAF rules to block the exploit vector before patching — protect all other users while remediation proceeds
Apply the vendor's security patch immediately — do not wait for a change window; critical application vulnerabilities warrant emergency change procedures
Rotate ALL credentials accessible to the compromised application: service accounts, API keys, database connection strings, secrets in configuration files, certificates
Preserve forensic evidence BEFORE any remediation: take a memory dump (WinPmem/DumpIt) and disk snapshot of the compromised server for legal/forensic preservation
short_term_actions: Review application logs from the earliest possible timestamp — not just detection time — to determine full scope: Get-ChildItem -Path C:\inetpub\logs -Recurse -Include *.log | Sort LastWriteTime -Descending | Select -First 10

Scan the compromised server for web shells and backdoors: Get-ChildItem -Path C:\inetpub\wwwroot -Recurse -Include *.aspx,*.php,*.jsp,*.ashx | Where {$_.LastWriteTime -gt (Get-Date).AddDays(-30)} | Select FullName,LastWriteTime
Notify legal and compliance teams if the exposed application processed regulated data (PII, PHI, PCI DSS cardholder data)
prevention: Establish a vulnerability management SLA: critical CVEs patched within 24-72 hours of vendor release
Deploy a WAF with virtual patching capability in front of all internet-facing applications as a secondary defense layer
Conduct quarterly external penetration testing and monthly authenticated vulnerability scans against public-facing infrastructure
Implement network segmentation so compromised DMZ systems cannot directly reach internal AD and database resources
accounts_at_risk: All service accounts and application credentials stored on or accessible from the exploited system — treat as fully compromised

immediate_actions: Block all phishing domains and URLs at the email gateway, DNS sinkhole, and web proxy immediately — extract indicators from email headers and message body

Search for delivery of similar phishing messages across the organization and notify all recipients: use email gateway log search or Microsoft Purview Content Search for the sender domain/subject pattern
Reset credentials for all users confirmed to have clicked the phishing link or opened and interacted with the attachment
Remove the phishing email from all mailboxes: in Microsoft 365 use: Search-UnifiedAuditLog then New-ComplianceSearchAction -ActionName Purge -PurgeType HardDelete in Security & Compliance Center
short_term_actions: Enable Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Safe Links and Safe Attachments (or equivalent) — all links should be rewritten and attachment-detonated before delivery
Enable DMARC, DKIM, and SPF for all organizational domains: publish DMARC record at minimum p=quarantine to reject spoofed messages
Conduct targeted security awareness training for all users who received this phishing campaign within 48 hours of the incident
prevention: Deploy Advanced Threat Protection with sandboxed attachment detonation for all inbound email
Enforce MFA on all email and VPN access so credential theft via phishing does not immediately enable account takeover
Conduct regular phishing simulation campaigns and use results to target security awareness training at highest-risk users
accounts_at_risk: All users who interacted with the phishing content — any credentials entered on phishing sites must be treated as fully compromised

immediate_actions: IMMEDIATELY disconnect all affected systems from the network — remove network cable and disable Wi-Fi; do NOT power off systems (memory evidence will be lost, and some ransomware variants trigger wipers on shutdown)
DO NOT pay ransom without engaging a specialist ransomware IR firm — check nomoreransom.org for free decryptors before making any payment decision
Preserve forensic evidence before any remediation: collect memory images (WinPmem, DumpIt) and disk images (dd or forensic imager) of affected systems for legal preservation and root cause analysis
Notify CISO, legal counsel, and executive leadership immediately — ransomware incidents trigger mandatory breach notification obligations (GDPR 72h, HIPAA, US state breach laws)
short_term_actions: Test clean backup restores in an ISOLATED environment before touching production — verify backups were not also encrypted or corrupted by the ransomware actor
Identify the ransomware variant via file extension, ransom note, and ID Ransomware (id-ransomware.malwarehunterteam.com)
Contact FBI IC3 (ic3.gov) and CISA (report.cisa.gov) — law enforcement may have decryption keys from prior takedowns
Identify and fully remediate the initial access vector before restoring any systems to prevent re-infection
prevention: Maintain offline, air-gapped backups that cannot be reached by ransomware — follow the 3-2-1 rule: 3 copies, 2 media types, 1 offsite
Deploy anti-ransomware protection in EDR (Windows Defender Controlled Folder Access, SentinelOne Rollback, CrowdStrike Falcon Complete)
Segment the network so ransomware cannot reach file servers, backup systems, and DCs from a single compromised endpoint
accounts_at_risk: All accounts on affected systems — ransomware actors routinely dump credentials before deploying encryption; treat entire environment as compromised

immediate_actions: Immediately verify if Volume Shadow Copies still exist: vssadmin list shadows — if deleted, recovery must come from external backups; do NOT attempt restore from the same environment if it is compromised
Check BCD store for tampering: bcdedit /enum all — look for disabled recovery options or modified boot entries that prevent safe-mode boot
Check external/offline backup integrity immediately — test restore of at least one critical system to an ISOLATED environment before trusting any backup
Enable VSS protection going forward: reg add HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\SystemRestore /v DisableSR /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f && vssadmin resize shadowstorage /For=C: /On=C: /MaxSize=20GB
short_term_actions: Enable Controlled Folder Access in Windows Defender to block ransomware from deleting shadow copies: Set-MpPreference -EnableControlledFolderAccess Enabled
Restrict vssadmin and wmic shadowcopy delete for non-administrator accounts via AppLocker path rules
Configure persistent shadow copies on all critical servers with minimum 30-day retention and at least one off-host copy
prevention: Implement immutable backups via Veeam Hardened Repository, Rubrik, or AWS S3 Object Lock — immutable backups cannot be deleted even with admin credentials
Block vssadmin.exe and wmic.exe for non-administrators via AppLocker
Create a real-time SIEM alert for vssadmin delete shadows or wmic shadowcopy delete commands — these should never run in normal operations
accounts_at_risk: Recovery capability for ALL systems — shadow copy deletion is a pre-encryption stage affecting the entire environment's recoverability

immediate_actions: Disable LLMNR immediately via Group Policy: Computer Config > Admin Templates > Network > DNS Client > 'Turn off multicast name resolution' = Enabled
Disable NetBIOS over TCP/IP for all adapters: Set-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\NetBT\Parameters\Interfaces\Tcpip_*' -Name NetbiosOptions -Value 2
Enable SMB signing on ALL systems: Set-SmbServerConfiguration -RequireSecuritySignature $True -Force && Set-SmbClientConfiguration -RequireSecuritySignature $True -Force

Rotate credentials for all accounts whose NTLM challenge-response hashes were captured during the poisoning window — identify affected accounts by correlating LLMNR traffic timestamps with user logon activity
short_term_actions: Disable WPAD (Web Proxy Auto-Discovery) which is also commonly poisoned: reg add 'HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Internet Settings\Wpad' /v WpadOverride /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
Enable Extended Protection for Authentication (EPA) on all IIS and Exchange servers to prevent NTLM relay to HTTP services
Enforce LDAP signing and channel binding on all Domain Controllers to block NTLM relay to LDAP: set Domain Controller: LDAP server signing requirements = Require signing in Group Policy
prevention: Disable LLMNR and NetBIOS globally via Group Policy as a baseline security configuration
Require SMB signing on all systems as a domain-wide GPO
Enable Extended Protection for Authentication (EPA) on all web services (IIS, Exchange, ADFS)
accounts_at_risk: Accounts whose NTLM hashes were captured — typically accounts that made file, print, or name-resolution requests from affected network segments during the attack window

immediate_actions: Identify the enumeration scope: review LDAP query logs and EID 4661 (object handle requested) for bulk group membership queries from the incident window: Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security';Id=4661} | Where {$_.Message -like '*group*'} | Group {$_.Properties[4].Value} | Sort Count -Descending

Check for BloodHound/SharpHound collection artifacts on affected hosts: Get-ChildItem -Recurse -Include *BloodHound*,*SharpHound*,*_computers.json,*_groups.json C:\ 2>$null | Select FullName,LastWriteTime
Alert privileged account holders that the attacker has full domain group topology — assume they know all attack paths to Domain Admins and high-value targets
short_term_actions: Enable LDAP query audit on Domain Controllers: auditpol /set /subcategory:"Directory Service Access" /success:enable — generates EID 4661 for AD object reads
Create SIEM detection: >100 LDAP queries for group membership objects within 60 seconds from a single non-DC source
Deploy Microsoft Defender for Identity — BloodHound/SharpHound collection is detected as a built-in alert ('Reconnaissance using directory services queries')
prevention: Restrict read access on sensitive AD attributes (adminCount, ms-DS-AllowedToDelegateTo) to administrators only via ACL hardening
Deploy honeypot domain group accounts that should never be queried — any LDAP read on them triggers an alert
Implement tiered admin model so group membership enumeration does not reveal direct attack paths to Domain Admins
accounts_at_risk: No direct credential risk from enumeration alone — but attacker now has a complete attack path map to privileged accounts; prioritize blocking those paths

immediate_actions: Identify accounts enumerated: review EID 4661 and LDAP query logs for bulk user object enumeration from the incident window — check for ADRecon, ldapdomaindump, or net user /domain patterns
Search for domain enumeration tool artifacts: Get-ChildItem -Recurse -Include adrecon*,domain_users.json,domain_computers.json,ldapdomaindump* C:\ 2>$null | Select FullName,LastWriteTime
Alert privileged account holders that their account details (username, group memberships, last logon) are known to the attacker — watch for targeted credential attacks against those accounts
short_term_actions: Enable DS Access audit: auditpol /set /subcategory:"Directory Service Access" /success:enable — generates EID 4661 for LDAP object reads
Create SIEM detection: >50 EID 4661 events for user objects within 30 seconds from a single non-DC source
Review LDAP ACLs — restrict read access on sensitive user attributes (description fields often contain credentials, ms-DS-AllowedToDelegateTo) to administrators only
prevention: Restrict AD read permissions for standard users on sensitive user object attributes via ACL modification
Deploy honeypot user accounts that should never be queried — any LDAP read triggers an immediate alert
Deploy Microsoft Defender for Identity for LDAP reconnaissance detection
accounts_at_risk: No direct credential risk from discovery alone — enumerated account details enable targeted follow-on attacks; prioritize securing discovered privileged accounts

immediate_actions: Block identified exfiltration endpoints at the firewall immediately — check for large outbound transfers to cloud storage (Dropbox, Mega, Google Drive), paste sites, or unusual IPs/domains

Capture and analyze network logs from the suspected exfiltration timeframe — look for DNS tunneling patterns: unusually long queries (>100 chars), high-frequency requests, excessive TXT record queries
Determine what data was exfiltrated: cross-reference exfiltration timestamps with file access audit logs (EID 4663), SharePoint audit logs, and DLP alerts
Notify legal and compliance teams if PII, PHI, or regulated data was exfiltrated — mandatory breach notification timelines begin at point of discovery
short_term_actions: Deploy DNS inspection/sinkholing to detect tunneling: route all DNS through an inspecting resolver and alert on queries >63 characters per label or >10 queries/second to a single domain
Implement egress filtering — allow only required outbound protocols (HTTPS via authenticated proxy) and block all others by default
Deploy DLP on email gateway and web proxy to detect and block sensitive data transmission going forward
prevention: Route all outbound traffic through an authenticated web proxy — block direct internet access from endpoints
Deploy a DNS security gateway (Cisco Umbrella, Cloudflare Gateway) with tunneling detection
Classify sensitive data and apply DLP policies with automatic blocking of unauthorized transmission
accounts_at_risk: Accounts that accessed exfiltrated data — verify via EID 4663 (file access) correlated with the exfiltration timestamp to determine data exposure scope

immediate_actions: Block outbound DNS to all resolvers except your authorized corporate resolvers immediately — this stops active DNS tunneling: New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName 'Block Direct DNS' -Direction Outbound -Protocol UDP -RemotePort 53 -Action Block (then allow only your resolvers)
Block outbound ICMP tunneling: New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName 'Block Outbound ICMP' -Direction Outbound -Protocol ICMPv4 -Action Block
Analyze network packet captures from the incident period for data-encoding patterns: base64 strings in DNS query names, unusually large ICMP payloads, high-volume FTP transfers
Identify data scope: determine what files or data were accessible to the attacker during the exfiltration window using EID 4663 file access auditing
short_term_actions: Enable full DNS query logging on all internal resolvers and forward to SIEM
Deploy network DLP to inspect outbound HTTP traffic for encoded sensitive data patterns
Block FTP (TCP 21) and raw socket protocols at egress unless operationally required
prevention: Block direct outbound DNS from endpoints — enforce use of corporate resolvers that log and inspect all queries
Deploy a DNS security solution (Palo Alto DNS Security, Cisco Umbrella) with tunneling detection capability
Apply strict egress filtering for all non-standard protocols at the perimeter firewall
accounts_at_risk: Accounts with access to the data that was exfiltrated — review file/share permissions and access logs on affected data stores

immediate_actions: Identify all files downloaded during the incident window: review EID 4688 process creation events for certutil -urlcache, bitsadmin /transfer, PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest/DownloadFile, and curl/wget invocations

Quarantine all files downloaded by attacker processes and submit to sandbox for behavioral analysis: Get-ChildItem C:\Windows\Temp,C:\Users\*\AppData\Local\Temp -Recurse | Where {$_.LastWriteTime -gt (Get-Date).AddDays(-7)} | Select FullName,LastWriteTime,Length
Block identified download URLs and IPs at the web proxy and firewall
Scan all affected systems with an updated EDR/AV to detect any tools that were downloaded and may still be present
short_term_actions: Block certutil.exe network access via Windows Defender Firewall: New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName 'Block certutil outbound' -Direction Outbound -Program 'C:\Windows\System32\certutil.exe' -Action Block
Implement authenticated web proxy with TLS inspection to intercept and scan all HTTPS downloads
Enable Application Reputation (SmartScreen) to block downloads of unsigned or low-reputation executables
prevention: Block LOLBin-based downloads via AppLocker: deny certutil.exe, mshta.exe, bitsadmin.exe from making outbound network connections
Apply WDAC to block execution of downloaded executables from user-writable paths (Temp, AppData, Downloads)
Alert on outbound HTTP/HTTPS connections from cmd.exe, powershell.exe, certutil.exe, and bitsadmin.exe via proxy logs
accounts_at_risk: Account under which the download was performed — check EID 4688 SubjectUserName from the incident window

immediate_actions: Block mshta.exe from making outbound network connections via Windows Firewall: New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName 'Block mshta outbound' -Direction Outbound -Program 'C:\Windows\System32\mshta.exe' -Action Block

Identify all mshta.exe executions during the incident window: Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security';Id=4688} | Where {$_.Properties[5].Value -like '*mshta*'} | Select TimeCreated,@{N='CmdLine';E={$_.Properties[8].Value}},@{N='User';E={$_.Properties[1].Value}}
Analyze any HTA files executed — extract from disk or reconstruct from process memory and submit to sandbox for behavioral analysis
Search for mshta-based persistence: check Run keys, scheduled tasks, and startup folders for mshta.exe invocations
short_term_actions: Disable mshta.exe via AppLocker Publisher rule or WDAC policy — mshta.exe has no legitimate end-user use case in most enterprise environments
Deploy ASR rule to block mshta.exe from launching child processes: Set-MpPreference -AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Ids 3b576869-a4ec-4529-8536-b80a7769e899 -AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Actions Enabled
Enable command-line logging for all process creation events: reg add HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\Audit /v ProcessCreationIncludeCmdLine_Enabled /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
prevention: Block mshta.exe execution via AppLocker for all non-administrative users — it has no common legitimate user-facing function
Create a SIEM alert on any mshta.exe execution — treat every instance as suspicious until proven otherwise
Deploy ASR rules to restrict mshta.exe from spawning child processes and making network connections
accounts_at_risk: Account that executed mshta.exe — check Sysmon EID 1 or EID 4688 User field from the incident window

immediate_actions: Identify all regsvr32.exe executions with remote URLs (Squiblydoo technique) during the incident: Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security';Id=4688} | Where {$_.Properties[8].Value -like '*regsvr32*' -and ($_.Properties[8].Value -like '*/i:http*' -or $_.Properties[8].Value -like '*/i:ftp*')}
Block regsvr32.exe from making outbound network connections: New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName 'Block regsvr32 outbound' -Direction Outbound -Program 'C:\Windows\System32\regsvr32.exe' -Action Block
Analyze any COM scriptlets (.sct files) loaded via regsvr32 — extract from web proxy cache or process memory and submit to sandbox
short_term_actions: Deploy ASR rule to block regsvr32 from loading COM scriptlets from the internet: Set-MpPreference -AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Ids b2b3f03d-6a65-4f7b-a9c7-1c7ef74a9ba4 -AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Actions Enabled
Create a SIEM alert: regsvr32.exe with /i: flag pointing to http/https/ftp URLs — this Squiblydoo bypass pattern has no legitimate business use

Enable command-line process audit logging if not already active: reg add HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\Audit /v ProcessCreationIncludeCmdLine_Enabled /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
prevention: Apply AppLocker Publisher rules to restrict regsvr32.exe to only registering locally-signed DLLs
Block regsvr32.exe network access at the firewall as standard hardening configuration
Deploy WDAC policies to prevent loading of unsigned COM scriptlets via regsvr32
accounts_at_risk: Account under which regsvr32.exe was executed — check EID 4688 SubjectUserName from the incident window

immediate_actions: Activate upstream DDoS mitigation immediately — contact your ISP or CDN provider (Cloudflare Magic Transit, Akamai Prolexic, AWS Shield Advanced) to enable scrubbing at the network edge
Enable rate limiting on all public-facing services at the load balancer/firewall level: limit new connections per source IP and implement SYN cookies

Identify attack source characteristics (source IPs, protocol, port patterns) from firewall logs and implement temporary ACLs: New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName 'DDoS Block Range' -Direction Inbound -RemoteAddress <attacker_range> -Action Block
Verify EID 5152 (WFP blocked packet) and EID 4227 (TCP port exhaustion) rates as ongoing volumetric attack impact indicators
short_term_actions: Migrate public-facing services behind a DDoS-protected CDN or scrubbing center if not already in place
Implement BGP Flowspec or null routing for identified attack source prefixes with your upstream provider
Deploy SYN cookies on all load balancers and firewalls handling public traffic
prevention: Contract with a DDoS mitigation provider as baseline infrastructure — not after an attack occurs
Implement BCP38 (anti-spoofing) at your network edge to prevent your infrastructure being used for amplification attacks
Configure rate limiting and connection limits on all public-facing services as a standard security baseline
accounts_at_risk: No direct credential risk — service availability and business continuity are the primary impacts during a volumetric attack

immediate_actions: Identify the targeted service from EID 7011 (service transaction timeout) and application logs: Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='System';Id=7011} | Select TimeCreated,@{N='Service';E={$_.Properties[0].Value}}

Restart affected services to restore immediate availability: Restart-Service -Name W3SVC,WAS -Force — monitor for recurrence and check resource consumption: Get-Counter '\Processor(_Total)\% Processor Time' -SampleInterval 5
Enable connection rate limiting on affected applications: IIS example — set maxConnections in applicationHost.config under system.webServer/serverRuntime
Identify and block the attack source IPs from application access logs: review IIS/application logs for the source of high-volume requests and add temporary firewall blocks
short_term_actions: Deploy application-layer rate limiting at the WAF or load balancer level: per-IP request rate limits prevent single-source floods
Configure application request timeouts to defend against slow-rate attacks (Slowloris): set connection timeout to 60 seconds in IIS/Nginx/Apache
Enable HTTP flood detection in your WAF with automatic blocking for sources exceeding request rate thresholds
prevention: Deploy a WAF with application-layer DDoS protection in front of all web-facing applications
Configure auto-scaling for web tier resources so capacity automatically absorbs request floods
Implement CAPTCHA challenges for suspicious traffic patterns at the application layer
accounts_at_risk: No direct credential risk — service availability impact affects all users of the targeted application
